blocks.text: Module purpose

This module is a practical starting point for anyone who uses a work account, device or information. It explains the everyday choices that help keep an organization safe: checking an unexpected request, protecting a login, handling a file carefully and speaking up when something seems wrong. It focuses on what employees can do, rather than technical tasks handled by IT staff.
Why this matters at work

A security incident does not always begin with a complicated attack. It may start when someone reuses a password, opens an unexpected attachment, leaves a laptop unlocked or sends a file to the wrong person. One mistake can interrupt work, expose customer or staff information, lead to fraudulent payments and weaken trust. Reporting a concern early gives the organization a better chance to limit the damage and restore normal work.
Learning outcomes
What learners should be able to do
Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability using familiar workplace examples.
Spot common risks, including phishing, malware, weak passwords, excessive access and accidental information sharing.
Choose safer ways to use accounts, devices, email, websites and business information.
Follow the organization’s approved process when reporting a suspicious event or an accidental mistake.
Describe how a security incident could affect daily operations, privacy, trust and legal or contractual responsibilities.
Key terms

rows: Term
Plain-language explanation
Cybersecurity
The steps people and organizations take to protect devices, accounts, systems and information from misuse, damage or access by the wrong people.
Asset
Something the organization values and needs to protect, such as a laptop, login, customer record or business process.
Threat
Something that could cause harm. It might be a criminal, a malicious program or an event that disrupts a service.
Vulnerability
A weakness that could make it easier for a threat to cause harm, such as an unpatched device or a reused password.
Risk
The likelihood that a threat will take advantage of a weakness, together with the harm that could result.
Confidentiality
Keeping information visible only to people who are authorized to see it.
Integrity
Keeping information accurate and ensuring that changes are made only by authorized people.
Availability
Making sure authorized people can access systems and information when they need them.
Multi-factor authentication (MFA)
A sign-in check that uses more than one type of proof, such as a password plus an approval on a trusted device.
Malware
Software designed to spy on, damage, disrupt or gain unauthorized access to a device or system.

blocks.text: Main topics
Topics covered
Confidentiality, integrity and availability (the CIA triad)
Threats, vulnerabilities and risk
Accounts, identity and using only the access needed for a task
Devices, approved software and updates
Safe handling of business information
Recognizing and reporting suspicious activity
Cybersecurity as a shared responsibility across the workplace
Core ideas in everyday language
Confidentiality, integrity and availability

These three ideas help explain what security is protecting. Confidentiality is about who can see information. Integrity is about whether information stays accurate and is changed appropriately. Availability is about whether people can use systems and information when work requires them. For example, ransomware could lock staff out of files, change or encrypt the files, and—in some incidents—be linked to stolen copies of the information. That can affect all three areas at once.
Threats, weaknesses and risk

Imagine an employee receives a fake invoice from someone pretending to be a supplier. The message is the threat. If the employee skips the usual payment checks, that is a weakness the attacker may exploit. The risk is that money could be sent to the wrong account. Following the normal process, checking unusual requests and reporting weaknesses can reduce that risk.
Accounts and access

Use your own account and keep your sign-in details private. Do not approve an MFA prompt unless you started the sign-in yourself. People should have the access they need for their work, but no more than that. If your role changes, you no longer need particular access, or you notice access that seems unusual, contact the appropriate support or security team.
Devices, software and updates

Lock your screen when you step away, even for a short time. Install updates through the organization’s approved process, and do not switch off security tools unless authorized support staff ask you to. Unapproved software, unknown USB devices and browser extensions can introduce malware or expose information.
Handling information

Before sharing, storing or discussing work information, pause to check who needs it and whether the method is approved. Use the organization’s storage and collaboration tools, check recipients carefully and share only what is needed. Avoid putting sensitive work information into a personal account or an unapproved public service.
Reporting something suspicious

Tell the organization promptly if you notice a suspicious message, an unexpected login alert, possible malware, a lost device or information sent to the wrong person. Use the reporting channel your organization has approved. You do not need to be certain that an incident has occurred before asking for help. A quick, honest report can help the response team contain a problem sooner.
Workplace examples
You receive an unexpected email asking you to buy gift cards for a manager. Instead of replying, you call the manager using a number you already trust and check whether the request is genuine.
Your phone shows an MFA approval request, but you are not signing in. You deny the request and report it rather than approving it to make the alert go away.
You are leaving a laptop in a shared meeting room. You lock the screen and take the laptop with you or store it securely.
You are sending a spreadsheet with customer details to an external partner. You confirm the recipient, use the approved sharing method and remove information the partner does not need.

You open a suspicious link and the browser begins behaving strangely. You follow the organization’s incident instructions, contact support and share details of the message. Do not take extra technical steps unless the response team instructs you to.
Business impact examples
How a security mistake can affect the organization

rows: What went wrong
Possible effect on the business and people
An account is taken over
An attacker may access other systems, request or redirect payments, view private information and damage customer confidence.
Malware reaches a work device
The employee may be unable to work; shared systems could be affected; restoring devices and files can take time and money.
Information is changed without permission
Staff may make decisions using incorrect records, customers may receive wrong information and work may need to be repeated.
A confidential file is exposed
People may be harmed by the disclosure, and the organization may face complaints, contractual consequences, reputational damage or notification duties.
A concern is reported late
An attacker may have longer to access systems or information, making containment and recovery more difficult and costly.

blocks.text: Safer habits to use every day
Use a different password for each important account and turn on approved MFA.
Pause before acting on an unexpected link, attachment, payment change or urgent request; verify it through a trusted channel.
Lock your screen and keep devices secure in public or shared places.
Use approved software, storage, email and collaboration tools.
Check that information is going to the right people, and share only what they need.
Keep devices and applications updated through the organization’s approved process.
Report suspicious activity and mistakes promptly, even when you are not sure what happened.

The assessment is planned around three question banks: A, B and C, with 10 questions in each bank. Questions will include multiple-choice items and workplace scenarios. They will check understanding of the CIA triad, threats and weaknesses, account protection, device safety, information handling, incident reporting and business impact. The application is intended to record the bank used, the attempt, the learner’s answers and the score. Where possible, a repeat attempt should use a different bank.
Module summary

Cybersecurity is part of ordinary work, not just an IT responsibility. Use your own account, protect devices and information, check unexpected requests, use approved tools and report concerns quickly. These small habits help protect confidentiality, integrity and availability—and reduce the chance that an incident will disrupt work, cause financial loss or harm people.

Module purpose

This module helps employees handle messages and requests that may be trying to trick or pressure them. It covers how to spot common warning signs, check a request safely and report a concern. The aim is to help people pause and make a safe choice during normal work, whether the request arrives by email, text, phone or chat.
Why this matters at work

A convincing message can look routine: an invoice to approve, a document to review or a request from someone who appears to be a manager. If an employee is rushed into sharing a password, opening a harmful file or changing payment details, the effects can reach beyond one inbox. Work may be interrupted, money or information may be lost, and customers or colleagues may be affected. A quick report gives the organization more time to respond.
Learning outcomes
What learners should be able to do
Describe phishing and social engineering in plain language.
Recognize warning signs in emails, texts, phone calls and workplace chat.
Verify unusual requests through a trusted contact method before acting.
Choose a safe response to suspicious links, attachments and payment changes.
Explain how a successful scam could affect people and the organization.
Report a suspicious message or an accidental click promptly using the organization’s process.
Key terms

rows: Term
Plain-language explanation
Phishing
A deceptive message that pretends to come from a trusted person or organization to get information, money or access.
Social engineering
Using trust, pressure, curiosity or helpfulness to persuade someone to reveal information or take an unsafe action.
Spear phishing
A targeted phishing message written for a particular person, team or organization.
Business email compromise (BEC)
A scam that uses a real or impersonated business email account to request money, change payment details or obtain sensitive information.
Spoofing
Making a sender name, email address, phone number or website look as if it belongs to someone else.
Verification
Checking that a request is genuine through a separate, trusted route, such as a known phone number or internal directory.

blocks.text: Main topics
Topics covered
Phishing messages and common warning signs
Social engineering and impersonation
Urgency, authority and emotional pressure
Links, attachments and QR codes
Business email compromise and payment diversion
Safe verification and incident reporting
Understanding the main risks
Phishing messages

Phishing messages arrive by email, text, messaging apps, social media and sometimes phone calls. They may ask you to sign in, open a file, pay an invoice or confirm personal details. Some are obvious, but others copy a real organization’s branding and writing style. Check the actual sender address and the context of the request. A familiar logo or a display name alone does not prove that a message is genuine.
Social engineering

Social engineering targets human judgement rather than a software weakness. A caller may pretend to be IT support, a supplier or a senior manager. They might ask you to share a one-time code, approve a sign-in, install a tool or bypass a normal check. It is fine to pause, say you need to verify the request and contact the person using details you already trust.
Urgency and authority

Scammers often create pressure with phrases such as “act now,” “your account will be closed” or “the director needs this immediately.” They may also claim that the request is confidential. Pressure is a reason to slow down, especially when the request involves money, credentials, personal information or a change to a normal process. Follow the same approval steps even when the sender appears senior.
Links, attachments and QR codes

A link can lead to a fake sign-in page, and an attachment can contain harmful software or ask you to enable unsafe features. Before opening anything unexpected, check whether you were expecting it and whether the sender and request make sense. If unsure, use your organization’s approved reporting method. Do not enter work credentials after following a link you do not trust.
Business email compromise

In a payment diversion scam, an attacker may impersonate a supplier or compromise a real mailbox and ask for bank details to be changed. The message can fit into an existing conversation, which makes it harder to notice. Never rely on email alone for a payment change. Confirm it by calling a known number from your records and use the organization’s required approval process.
Verification and reporting

Verify a request using a separate route, not the phone number, link or reply address supplied in the suspicious message. Use a trusted directory, previously saved contact details or your organization’s normal process. Report suspicious messages even if you are uncertain. If you clicked a link, opened a file or shared information, report that promptly and explain what happened. Follow the instructions from your IT or security team; early reporting helps them decide what to do next.
Workplace examples
You receive an email that appears to be from your manager asking you to buy gift cards urgently. You contact the manager using a number already in your directory before doing anything.
A supplier emails new bank details just before an invoice is due. You call the supplier on a previously verified number and follow your organization’s payment approval process.
A text says your work account will be disabled unless you sign in through a link. You do not use the link; you go to the normal sign-in page or contact IT through the approved channel.
Someone claiming to be IT support asks for your MFA code over the phone. You do not share it and independently contact the help desk to confirm the call.
You open an unexpected attachment and then notice unusual behavior on your device. You report it immediately and follow the organization’s incident instructions.
Business impact examples
How a successful scam can affect the organization

rows: What may happen
Possible effect on people and the organization
An employee enters a password on a fake sign-in page
An attacker may use the account to access email or files, impersonate the employee, or try the same password elsewhere. Work may need to stop while access is secured.
A payment request is not independently checked
Money may be sent to a criminal-controlled account. The organization may face financial loss, recovery work and delays paying legitimate suppliers.
A harmful attachment is opened
Malware may disrupt a device or shared service. Staff may lose access to tools, and IT teams may need time to investigate and restore systems.
Sensitive information is sent to an impostor
Employees, customers or suppliers may face privacy harm. The organization may need to contain the exposure, contact affected people and manage legal or contractual obligations.
A suspicious message or mistake is reported late
A scam may have more time to spread or use an account. Containment and recovery can become more difficult, costly and disruptive.

blocks.text: Safer responses to use every day
Pause when a message asks for money, passwords, MFA codes, personal information or an unusual action.
Check the sender and the context; do not trust a display name or logo by itself.
Verify sensitive or unusual requests through a separate, known contact method.
Use the organization’s normal payment and approval procedures, even under time pressure.
Avoid opening unexpected links or attachments; report them through the approved channel.
Never share your password or one-time authentication code with someone who contacts you.
If you make a mistake, report it quickly and honestly so the response team can help.

Module summary

A suspicious message is easier to handle when you pause before acting. Check the request, verify it through a trusted route and report anything that concerns you. These simple steps can help protect accounts, money, information, daily operations and the trust people place in the organization.

Module purpose
Protect accounts by using strong authentication, managing passwords safely and understanding access permissions.

A sign in alert appears on your phone while you are making coffee. You did not try to log in. The safest response is not to approve it just to clear the notification. Deny the request, then report it using your organisation’s approved channel. Someone may have your password and be trying to get past the second sign in check.
Learning outcomes
Purpose and learning outcomes

This module is about keeping the right people in control of work accounts. It covers passwords and passphrases, multi factor authentication, password managers and access permissions, with clear steps for handling sign in alerts and account recovery.
Choose a strong, unique password or passphrase for a work account.
Explain how multi factor authentication adds a second check and what to do with an unexpected prompt.
Use only an organization approved password manager and account recovery process.
Recognize when access is broader than your role requires.
Respond to unfamiliar sign in alerts and report possible account compromise.
Key terms

rows: Term
Meaning at work
Password or passphrase
A secret used to prove who you are when signing in. A longer phrase that is hard to guess can be easier to remember than a short, complicated password.
Multi factor authentication (MFA)
A second proof of identity, such as an authenticator approval, security key or code, in addition to a password.
Password manager
An approved tool that stores and creates unique credentials so you do not have to reuse or remember each one.
Least privilege
Giving each person only the access needed for their current work.
Account recovery
The approved steps for regaining control of an account after losing access or suspecting it has been compromised.
Credential stuffing
An attack where criminals try passwords exposed from one service on other accounts.

blocks.text: Main topics
Practical guidance
Passwords that do not travel between accounts

Use a different password for each important account. If one service is breached, a unique password makes it harder for someone to use the same details elsewhere. Avoid predictable choices such as a name, birthday or common phrase. Use the organisation’s approved password manager if one is provided; never store work credentials in an unapproved note or personal account.
MFA prompts are a security decision

MFA can help block someone who knows your password, but it only works if you reject prompts you did not initiate. Never read a one time code to a caller or send it in chat. If you receive repeated prompts, deny them and contact IT or security through a known channel.
Access should match the job

Use your own account; shared logins make it difficult to tell who did what and to remove access when roles change. Ask for access through the proper approval process. If you no longer need a permission or notice access that seems excessive, report it rather than testing what it allows.
When an account may be at risk

If you entered a password on a page you now suspect was fake, or approve an unexpected prompt, report it quickly. Follow the organisation’s recovery instructions. Do not wait until you know whether the account was accessed; the support team can check sign in activity and advise on the next step.
Workplace examples
A realistic sign in moment
You receive an MFA approval request while you are not signing in. Deny it, then report it. Do not approve it to make the notification disappear.
A coworker asks to borrow your login because they cannot access a shared folder. Do not share your account; help them request their own access.
You reused a personal password for a work service and hear that the personal service had a breach. Tell IT or security and follow the reset guidance.
A login alert shows a location or device you do not recognize. Use the link or reporting route provided by your organization, not a link in an unexpected email.
Business impact examples
How a mistake could affect the business

rows: Situation
Possible effect
Reused password is exposed
An attacker may try the same password on work email or file services, potentially exposing business records and disrupting access.
MFA request is approved by mistake
A criminal may gain access to the account, impersonate the employee or attempt payment and data theft.
Shared account is used
The organisation may be unable to identify the person responsible, investigate a change or remove access safely.
Excessive access remains active
A compromised or misused account may reach more systems or information than the employee needs.

blocks.text: Habits to take back to work
Use unique credentials and the approved password manager.
Approve an MFA request only when you initiated the sign in.
Keep recovery information current through the approved process.
Never share your login or one time code.
Request access for your own account and report access that is no longer needed.
Report unexpected alerts and possible credential exposure promptly.

This module helps employees make careful decisions about work and personal information. It follows information through its everyday life cycle and shows how to share only what is needed, use approved storage and report a possible privacy incident.
Module purpose

You are sending a spreadsheet to a project partner. Before attaching it, you check the recipient, confirm the partner is authorized to receive it and remove columns they do not need. That small pause can prevent information about staff or customers from going to the wrong person.
Learning outcomes
Purpose and learning outcomes

This module helps employees make careful decisions about work and personal information. It follows information through its everyday life cycle and shows how to share only what is needed, use approved storage and report a possible privacy incident.
Identify personal, confidential and business sensitive information.
Use the organization’s classification and handling rules.
Apply need to know when accessing or sharing information.
Choose approved ways to store, send, retain and dispose of records.
Recognize and report a possible privacy breach or mistaken disclosure.
Key terms

rows: Term
Meaning at work
Personal information
Information or an opinion about an identified person, or a person who can reasonably be identified.
Sensitive information
Information that could cause greater harm if exposed, such as health, identity, financial or confidential business records.
Classification
A label or handling category that tells staff how information should be protected.
Need to know
Access is given because someone needs the information for an authorized work task.
Data minimization
Collecting, using or sharing only the information needed for the stated purpose.
Privacy incident
An event that may expose personal information to someone who should not see it or otherwise affect its proper handling.

blocks.text: Main topics
Practical guidance
Collect and use with a clear purpose

Before collecting details, consider whether they are actually needed for the task. Use information only for an authorized work purpose and follow the organization’s privacy notice, policy and retention rules. Extra copies or fields can create extra risk without helping the work.
Classify before you share

Use the organization’s labels and handling instructions. If you are unsure whether a file is confidential or contains personal information, treat it carefully and ask the data owner or privacy contact. Check recipients, permissions and attachment contents before sending.
Store and keep information in approved places

Use authorized business systems rather than personal email, personal cloud drives or removable media. Apply sharing permissions carefully, especially for links that allow access to anyone. Keep records only for the period required by policy or law, then dispose of them using the approved method.
A mistake is still reportable

If you send a file to the wrong person, expose a shared link or find information in an unexpected location, report it promptly. Do not try to hide the mistake or contact external recipients unless your organization’s response team instructs you. Early reporting helps limit further access and assess who may be affected.
Workplace examples
Follow the information life cycle
A team asks you to gather extra customer details “just in case.” Check whether the details are needed and authorize before collecting them.
A colleague requests access to a staff file but does not work on the relevant task. Confirm the need and approval before sharing.
You create a link to a report. Set access for the intended recipients only and check whether the link can be forwarded.
You notice an old shared folder containing records that are no longer needed. Ask the data owner to apply the retention and disposal process.
Business impact examples
How a mistake could affect the business

rows: Situation
Possible effect
File sent to the wrong recipient
Customers or staff may face embarrassment, fraud or other privacy harm. The organization may need to contain access, assess notification obligations and respond to complaints.
Overly broad link permissions
Information may be viewed or copied by people outside the intended group, creating exposure that is hard to reverse.
Unneeded records are kept indefinitely
The organization has more information to protect and may face a larger impact if a device, account or service is compromised.
Incident is not reported
An exposed link or mistaken disclosure may remain active longer, increasing the number of people affected and the effort needed to respond.

blocks.text: Habits to take back to work
Collect only what the task needs and use it for an authorized purpose.
Check the information label and recipient permissions before sharing.
Use approved business storage and transfer tools.
Follow retention rules; do not keep extra copies for convenience.
Report a misdirected email, exposed link or other privacy concern quickly.
Quick self check

Done

I know how to report a possible privacy incident.

This module focuses on the internet choices employees make during a normal workday: opening a website, joining Wi Fi, downloading a file or connecting remotely. It explains what to check and when to use the organization’s approved tools.
Module purpose

You are at an airport and need to send a work file before boarding. A free Wi Fi network has a name that looks like the airport’s official network. Instead of guessing, use your organization’s approved connection method or wait until you can connect safely. Convenience is not worth exposing a work session.
Learning outcomes
Purpose and learning outcomes

This module focuses on the internet choices employees make during a normal workday: opening a website, joining Wi Fi, downloading a file or connecting remotely. It explains what to check and when to use the organization’s approved tools.
Recognize safer website connections and suspicious web addresses.
Choose an appropriate connection for work, including while travelling.
Use VPN and remote access only as instructed by the organization.
Handle downloads and browser warnings safely.
Recognize signs of online scams and report concerns.
Key terms

rows: Term
Meaning at work
HTTPS
A web connection that uses encryption between the browser and website. It does not, on its own, prove the website is trustworthy.
Public Wi Fi
A wireless network shared with the public, such as in an airport, cafe or hotel.
VPN
An approved service that creates a protected connection to an organization’s network or resources.
Browser warning
A notice that a connection, certificate, download or website may be unsafe or unusual.
Domain name
The part of a web address that identifies the website. Look carefully for misspellings or extra words.
Remote access
A way to connect to work systems from outside the organization’s usual network, under approved security controls.

blocks.text: Main topics
Practical guidance
Read the address, not just the page

A fake website can copy a familiar sign in page. Check the domain carefully and use a saved bookmark or the organization’s normal app rather than a link in an unexpected message. HTTPS helps protect data in transit, but scammers can also use HTTPS, so it is not a guarantee that a site is legitimate.
Choose a connection with care

For work, follow the organization’s Wi Fi and remote access rules. Public Wi Fi may be impersonated or monitored. If policy allows work over a public network, use the approved VPN or secure connection and avoid sensitive tasks when you cannot establish a trusted connection. Do not bypass warnings to get online.
Treat downloads as a decision

Download work software and files only from sources approved by your organization. Be cautious if a website asks you to install a browser extension, enable macros or turn off security settings. If a file is unexpected, verify it with the sender through a trusted channel.
Remote access should stay inside approved tools

Use only the remote access method configured by your organization. Do not install a personal remote desktop app or expose work systems to the internet yourself. If the connection behaves unexpectedly or you see repeated sign in prompts, stop and contact IT through the normal support route.
Workplace examples
Online choices in a workday
A hotel network asks you to install a “Wi Fi security certificate” before connecting. Do not install it unless your IT team has confirmed it is required.
A link opens a familiar looking sign in page, but the web address contains an extra word. Close it and report the message that sent you there.
A browser warns that a work website’s connection cannot be verified. Do not ignore the warning; contact support or use the approved route.
A free converter website asks you to upload a confidential work document. Do not upload it to an unapproved service; use a sanctioned tool.
Business impact examples
How a mistake could affect the business

rows: Situation
Possible effect
Credentials entered on a fake site
An attacker may use the account to access email, documents or other connected services, leading to further compromise and response work.
Sensitive work over an untrusted connection
Information or active sessions may be exposed, putting customer or business data at risk.
Unapproved software is installed
Malicious or poorly secured software may introduce malware, capture data or create a route into work systems.
Browser warning is bypassed
The employee may continue to a site with a certificate or connection problem, increasing the chance of interception or impersonation.

blocks.text: Habits to take back to work
Use bookmarks or known addresses for important work services.
Remember that HTTPS is helpful but does not prove a site is genuine.
Follow your organization’s guidance for public Wi Fi, VPN and remote access.
Do not bypass browser or security warnings without advice from IT.
Use approved sources for downloads and report suspicious pages.
Quick self-check

Done
I check web addresses before entering work credentials.
I know what connection method to use when working away from the office.
I do not install unapproved extensions, certificates or remote access tools.
I understand that HTTPS alone does not make a website trustworthy.
I know how to report a suspicious site or connection warning.

Multiple choice items will be mixed with everyday work scenarios. This module turns device security into a practical routine. It covers screen locks, software updates, endpoint protection, USB devices, physical security and backups, with attention to what employees should do when a device goes missing or behaves strangely.
Module purpose

You step away from a shared desk to take a call. Locking the screen takes a second, but it prevents someone nearby from opening your work or sending a message as you. Good device security often comes down to small actions repeated at the right moment.
Learning outcomes
Purpose and learning outcomes

This module turns device security into a practical routine. It covers screen locks, software updates, endpoint protection, USB devices, physical security and backups, with attention to what employees should do when a device goes missing or behaves strangely.
Secure a work device when stepping away or travelling.
Explain why approved updates and security software matter.
Handle removable media safely.
Protect devices in shared and public locations.
Know what to do if a device is lost, stolen or behaving unusually.
Key terms

rows: Term
Meaning at work
Screen lock
A control that requires sign in again after a device is unattended.
Security update
A software or device change that fixes known problems and may improve protection.
Endpoint protection
Approved security software that helps detect or block malicious activity on a work device.
Removable media
Portable storage such as a USB drive or external disk.
Physical security
Steps that prevent unauthorized people from reaching, taking or tampering with equipment.
Backup
A separate recoverable copy of information kept according to the organization’s policy.

blocks.text: Main topics
Practical guidance
A device left unattended is still in use

Lock your screen whenever you step away, including in a meeting room or shared workspace. Keep laptops and phones with you or secured when travelling. Do not leave equipment visible in a parked car. Avoid lending a work device or allowing another person to use your signed in session.
Updates and protection need to stay on

Install updates through the process your organization provides. Updates can fix security weaknesses, so postponing them indefinitely can leave devices easier to attack. Do not disable antivirus, endpoint protection, encryption or management settings. If a tool blocks something you need, contact IT rather than working around it.
Unknown USB devices are not a shortcut

A USB drive can carry harmful software or expose stored information. Use only organization approved devices and follow the rules for transferring files. Do not plug in a drive you find in a car park or receive unexpectedly, even if it has a familiar label.
If a device goes missing

Report a lost or stolen work device immediately, even if you think it is password protected. Share where and when it went missing and what work information it may contain. Follow the support team’s instructions; they may be able to lock the device or protect accounts. Do not try to investigate or recover it in a way that puts you at risk.
Workplace examples
A day with a work device
You are leaving a laptop at a hot desk for a short meeting. Lock it, and take it with you or store it in an approved secure place.
A pop up says your security software is slowing down the computer and offers to disable it. Do not follow it; contact IT.
A visitor asks to borrow a USB cable and leaves a USB drive on your desk. Do not plug the drive in; use the approved file transfer route.
You cannot find your work phone after leaving a rideshare. Report it promptly so the organization can assess access and protect work data.
Business impact examples
How a mistake could affect the business

rows: Situation
Possible effect
Unlocked device is accessed
Someone may read email or files, change records or send messages using the employee’s identity.
Updates are delayed or security tools are disabled
Known weaknesses may remain open, increasing the chance of malware or unauthorized access and creating downtime.
Unknown USB is connected
Malware may infect the device or files may be copied without permission, leading to investigation and recovery work.
Lost device is reported late
There is more time for someone to access work accounts or information, and the organization has fewer options to limit exposure.

blocks.text: Habits to take back to work
Lock the screen whenever you leave a device unattended.
Keep devices physically secure at work, at home and while travelling.
Install approved updates and keep security tools enabled.
Use only approved USB devices and transfer methods.
Report lost equipment or unusual device behavior as soon as possible.
Follow backup instructions; do not create unapproved copies of work data.
Quick self check

rows: Ask yourself
Done
I lock my screen when I step away.
I know how updates are installed on my work devices.
I keep approved security tools enabled.
I do not connect unknown USB devices.
I know how to report a missing or suspicious device.

blocks.text: Assessment coverage
Assessment design

The three planned banks each contain 10 questions. They cover screen locking, updates, endpoint protection, removable media, physical security, lost devices and backups. Questions will mix short knowledge checks with scenarios such as an unknown USB drive or a missing phone. The application is intended to record the bank selected, attempt, answers, score and feedback and to choose another bank for repeat attempts when possible.

title: Module 7 – AI Literacy and AI Security

blocks.text: This module introduces employees to safe, thoughtful use of AI tools. It explains that AI generated outputs can be wrong or misleading, that prompts may contain sensitive information, and that people remain responsible for checking decisions and following workplace rules. This is learning content; it does not mean the project application will include AI features.
Module purpose

An AI assistant drafts a polished summary of a policy and includes a confident statement that you cannot find in the original. The writing sounds certain, but that does not make it correct. Before using the summary, check important details against an approved source and ask a qualified colleague if the decision matters.
Learning outcomes
Purpose and learning outcomes

This module introduces employees to safe, thoughtful use of AI tools. It explains that AI generated outputs can be wrong or misleading, that prompts may contain sensitive information, and that people remain responsible for checking decisions and following workplace rules. This is learning content; it does not mean the project application will include AI features.
Describe in simple terms what generative AI tools do and where they can help.
Recognize that generated information may be inaccurate, biased or incomplete.
Protect confidential and personal information when using AI tools.
Check output, sources and permissions before sharing or acting on it.
Recognize possible deepfake or impersonation attempts and verify important requests.
Key terms

rows: Term
Meaning at work
Generative AI
A type of AI that creates content such as text, images, audio or code from instructions and patterns learned from data.
Prompt
The instruction or information a person gives an AI tool.
Hallucination
A confident sounding output that is false, unsupported or made up.
Human review
A person checks an AI output for accuracy, context, bias and appropriateness before relying on it.
Deepfake
Synthetic or altered media that can make a person appear to say or do something they did not.
Approved AI tool
A tool the organization has assessed and permitted for specified work tasks.

blocks.text: Main topics
Practical guidance
Start with the approved tool and task

Before using AI for work, check whether the organization permits the tool and the type of task. Public tools may retain or process prompts under their own terms. Do not paste customer records, employee details, credentials, confidential plans, source code or internal documents unless the organization has explicitly approved that use.
Treat output as a draft, not proof

AI may produce incorrect facts, citations, calculations or instructions. Check important claims against reliable sources and review the original material. Be especially careful with legal, financial, security, health or employment decisions. A human remains accountable for what is sent or acted on.
Look for privacy, bias and copyright concerns

Avoid asking an AI system to reveal or infer private information about a person. Check whether generated text or images could be biased, misleading or too similar to protected material. Follow workplace rules for attribution, copyright, record keeping and disclosure.
Verify unusual audio, video and messages

A voice or video call may be convincing and still be fake or manipulated. Treat urgent requests for money, credentials or confidential files like any other high risk request: stop and verify using a separate, trusted contact method. Report suspected impersonation or harmful AI use through the organization’s process.
Workplace examples
Four questions before using an AI output
Is this tool approved for the work I am doing? If you are unsure, check the organization’s guidance.
Does the prompt contain personal, confidential or security sensitive information? Remove it or do not proceed unless the tool and task are approved.
Can I verify the answer against an authoritative source? Check key facts, calculations, references and recommendations.
Could someone mistake this output for a real person’s words or a verified decision? Label or review it as required by workplace policy.
Business impact examples
How a mistake could affect the business

rows: Situation
Possible effect
Confidential information is pasted into an unapproved tool
Information may be stored or processed outside the organization’s control, creating privacy, contractual or security concerns.
Incorrect AI output is used without checking
A wrong decision, customer response or security instruction may cause financial loss, rework, unfair treatment or operational disruption.
Biased or misleading output is shared
People may be treated unfairly, trust may be damaged and the organization may need to correct the decision or explain its process.
A deepfake request is treated as genuine
An employee may transfer funds, disclose information or change account details based on a fabricated voice or video.

blocks.text: Habits to take back to work
Use only AI tools and tasks approved by your organization.
Keep confidential data, credentials and personal information out of prompts unless specifically authorized.
Check important outputs against trusted sources before using or sharing them.
Keep a human responsible for consequential decisions.
Verify urgent money or access requests using a known contact method.
Report suspected AI enabled impersonation or harmful use.
Quick self check

rows: Ask yourself
Done
I know which AI tools, if any, my organization permits.
I understand that generated answers can be wrong or biased.
I avoid entering sensitive information into unapproved tools.
I check important outputs before relying on or sharing them.
I know how to verify a suspicious voice, video or message.

blocks.text: Assessment coverage
Assessment design

The planned assessment contains three banks of 10 questions each. It will cover approved use, accuracy and hallucinations, sensitive information, copyright and confidentiality, human review, bias, and deepfakes. Multiple choice items and workplace scenarios will check whether learners can make safe decisions. The application is intended to record the selected bank, attempt, answers, score and feedback, and use a different bank for a repeat attempt where available.

title: Module 8 – Incident Reporting and Cyber Hygiene

blocks.text: This module helps employees recognize when something may be wrong and report it clearly. It covers what to report, what information to share, how to follow containment instructions and how daily habits such as updates and backups support recovery.
Module purpose

You click a link in an email and realize a moment later that the address looks unusual. It is tempting to close the window and hope nothing happened. Report it instead. The response team can decide whether action is needed, and the details you provide may help protect other employees too.
Learning outcomes
Purpose and learning outcomes

This module helps employees recognize when something may be wrong and report it clearly. It covers what to report, what information to share, how to follow containment instructions and how daily habits such as updates and backups support recovery.
Recognize common events that should be reported.
Use the organization’s internal reporting route promptly.
Describe what happened clearly without investigating beyond one’s role.
Follow instructions from the response team and preserve relevant details.
Explain how updates, backups and routine security habits support recovery.
Key terms

rows: Term
Meaning at work
Security event
An activity or change that may be relevant to security but has not yet been confirmed as harmful.
Incident
An event that has affected or may affect accounts, devices, information or services and requires an organizational response.
Containment
Steps taken by authorized responders to limit the spread or impact of an incident.
Evidence
Relevant details that help responders understand what happened, such as a time, message or screenshot.
Backup
A protected copy of information used to restore work after loss or damage.
Cyber hygiene
Regular security habits, including updates, careful sharing, strong authentication and prompt reporting.

blocks.text: Main topics
Practical guidance
What should you report?

Report suspicious sign in alerts, suspected phishing, unusual device behavior, missing equipment, unexpected changes to files, possible data sent to the wrong person and any mistake involving a work account or device. You do not need to prove that an attack occurred. When in doubt, ask the security or IT team.
Use the organization’s reporting route

Use the internal channel your organization has provided, such as a report button, help desk, security mailbox or incident form. If the usual channel is unavailable, use the documented backup contact. Include what you observed, when it happened, which device or account was involved and what you did next.
Follow instructions and avoid making things worse

Once you report, follow the response team’s guidance. Do not delete messages, wipe devices, forward suspicious files broadly or post details publicly unless instructed. Avoid trying to investigate or fix the issue yourself. Some incidents require specific steps, so the response team should guide the response.
Routine habits help recovery

Install updates through the approved process, protect accounts with MFA, store work in approved locations and follow backup procedures. Backups are useful only when they are protected and can be restored. Employees should not change backup settings or create extra copies outside policy.
Workplace examples
A simple report should answer
What did you notice? Describe the message, alert, device behavior or information exposure in plain language.
When did it happen? Include the approximate time and time zone if you know it.
What did you do? Say whether you clicked, opened, replied, entered details or shared a file.
What is involved? Identify the work account, device, file or service, and follow the response team’s instructions.
Business impact examples
How a mistake could affect the business

rows: Situation
Possible effect
A suspicious message is reported quickly
The security team can warn others, block similar messages and check whether any account or device needs attention.
A possible data exposure is reported
The organization can limit access, assess who may be affected and meet any relevant response or notification duties.
A device issue is hidden or self fixed
Important details may be lost, the cause may remain active, and the response team may have less time to contain it.
Updates and backups are neglected
Known weaknesses may remain open and recovery may take longer if important files or systems are damaged.

blocks.text: Habits to take back to work
Report suspicious activity and mistakes as soon as you notice them.
Be clear about what happened and what actions you took.
Use the organization’s internal channel and follow the response team’s instructions.
Do not delete, forward widely, wipe or investigate unless instructed.
Install approved updates and follow backup and storage procedures.
Keep incident details within approved channels.
Quick self check

rows: Ask yourself
Done
I know the internal channel for reporting security concerns.
I would report an accidental click or disclosure promptly.
I can describe what happened and what I did next.
I will follow responder instructions instead of trying to investigate.
I know that updates and protected backups support recovery.

blocks.text: Assessment coverage
Assessment design

Banks A, B and C each contain 10 questions. They cover what counts as an incident, when and where to report, useful reporting details, containment instructions, updates, backups and daily cyber hygiene. Learners will answer multiple choice and workplace scenario questions. The application is intended to record the bank, attempt, answers, score and feedback and choose a different bank on a repeat attempt when possible.
